Hydraulic Elevator

An academic concept for a single-piston hydraulic lift, sized against seven governing-equation plots. A course proposal only, never built or approved for use.

Role
Design Engineer, Team of 4
Timeline
One semester, Fluid Mechanics
Tools
Hand Calcs, MATLAB, SolidWorks
Status
Academic proposal, not fabricated
Isometric view of the finalized single-piston elevator assembly
Outcome

A team-of-four Fluid Mechanics design study that selected a single-piston cylinder by weighted decision matrix and sized it to a 3 in bore at 53.7 psi, reaching full 12 in extension in ~20 bicycle-pump strokes. Every structural check cleared its allowable.

This design was never fabricated, tested, or approved for use. It exists only as a course deliverable. Lifting a person on compressed gas in Schedule 40 PVC carries real rupture risk that a course-level safety factor doesn't retire; a build would need a properly rated pressure vessel.

My contribution
  • Evaluated the three candidate lift architectures against safety, feasibility, and leakage risk
  • Derived the governing equations for the selected single-piston mechanism
  • Sized the piston, rod, and platform through closed-form hand calculations
  • Modeled the complete assembly in CAD
  • Produced all engineering drawings and the bill of materials
Objective & Constraints
Motion
6 to 12 in of travel, stoppable and holdable at any intermediate height for 5 minutes
Load
200 to 300 lb human load target, designed to a 379.5 lb force with a 1.15 safety factor, a course-level margin only, not sufficient for an actual human-rated lift
Working fluid
Water, air, or a combination only, actuated by a standard bicycle pump
Build
Off-the-shelf stock, one week to build if ever approved
Development

We evaluated three hydraulic lift architectures against safety, feasibility, stability, leakage risk, and efficiency.

Scissor lift
Rejected: actuator force exceeds twice the design load at low angles, and multiple pin joints raise shear-failure risk.
Telescopic lift
Rejected: decreasing stage areas demand rising pressure across stages, multiplying sealing interfaces and leak risk.
Single piston cylinder: selected
Chosen: direct F = PA relationship, one stage, fewest seals, and the highest score on the weighted decision matrix.
Engineering Decision

The diameter and pump-effort curves both level off near 3 in, so we sized the bore to 3 in Schedule 40 PVC instead of the 2.8 in minimum. That gives about 53.7 psi working pressure and about 20 pump strokes to full height. Hoop stress had margin, but end caps, joints, fittings, buckling, and dynamic loads were not checked, and PVC is not rated for compressed gas.

Required diameter vs. pressure, output force vs. diameter, and pump strokes vs. working pressure
Calculations

Checked with hand calculations and parametric plots only, never built or tested. Every structural check passed under the stated assumptions, including the 18 x 18 in plywood platform staying under the 0.1 in deflection limit. Seals, fittings, joints, and dynamic loading were not covered.

Cylinder wall
0.5 in actual vs. 0.01 in min
Piston rod
1.5 in, >4x min buckling diameter
Platform deflection
Under 0.1 in limit
Tie rods
Well below allowable stress
Buckling load vs. rod length, total rod stress vs. load eccentricity, and tensile stress vs. tie-rod diameter
Planned validation criteria (not yet tested)
  • Vertical displacement of 6 to 12 in under the full 379.5 lb design force
  • 19 to 20 pump strokes (±2) to reach maximum height
  • Less than 0.5 in vertical drift holding maximum height for 5 minutes
  • No visible leakage at seals, fittings, or valves, and no permanent deformation after testing
